title: Thrum
excerpt: Thrum gives your AI coding agents one coordinator. It hands out the work, reviews what comes back and does the merging, and is set up to build and test the merged result before it pushes, so you can trust what reaches you.
content_html:
Stop babysitting your coding agents. They check each other's work, so you can trust what reaches you.

Your agents message each other, even when they run on different tools: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. No more pasting one agent's answer into another's window. Start with two: a coordinator you talk to, and a reviewer it creates when you ask. When the work grows, add agents and keep talking to one. You get decisions, not diffs to chase.

Install Thrum free

Free costs nothing and needs no account.

Or try Pro free for 14 days Watch the 2-minute walkthrough

Start your free 14-day trial today. Buying opens soon. We'll email you once when it does. No card for the trial. When it ends, Thrum goes back to Free and your data stays.

Free costs nothing and needs no account: your agents message each other, you talk to them in their own terminals or message them from My Inbox, and you watch them in the web UI. Pro is $15.00/month or $120.00/year. It lets you type to your agents from the web UI and lets them write memory and a work queue.

Agents check each other's work

An agent saying "done" is a claim, not a result. In Thrum, the claim is checked before it reaches you.

  • Your coordinator reviews each branch, and before it pushes a merge it's set up to build and test the merged result. You choose whether it asks you before each merge or merges routine changes itself.
  • Add a gate agent, an agent whose job is to run your tests on that merged code. Its verdict says what it measured and what it didn't. If no gate agent checked a merge, the record says so.
  • The agents that write the code (implementers) are told to start from a failing test, so a fix has something to prove.

In the video above, a reviewer on a different model reports two minor findings, and the coordinator confirms neither needs a change before anything reaches you.

If you run more than one coding agent

You don't need several agents already. Two are enough to start, and each one can run on whichever AI tool and model you choose.

You're the one carrying messages between them, checking what each one says it did, and remembering who is waiting on whom. With Thrum, they message each other, a reviewer checks what they say they did, and you talk to one coordinator.

Thrum is for developers running more than one coding agent on real code, who want to stay the one who decides. With two or three agents, Free has everything your agents need to work as a team. It costs nothing and needs no account. If your project is in a public repository, Pro is free too, for each one you register, as long as it stays public. You need a free account for that. How to get it

Many AI tools let one agent hand work to its own subagents or team. Thrum's messages go between full agents, each in its own session, on whichever supported tool it runs, and to you. If one agent and its helpers cover your work, you may not need more. Thrum is excellent when your agents run on more than one tool, or when you want one coordinator to talk to and an inbox of your own.

If you'd rather not build it yourself

If you want this functionality, you can build it yourself today. Claude Code is good at that, but you have to build it yourself, and you have to troubleshoot it. Thrum gives it to you out of the box, and that part is free.

Install Thrum

Your agents deploy, too

Ask your coordinator to add a deployer. It runs your scripted deploys. It's set up to deploy dev and staging on its own and to ask your coordinator before production. Afterwards it checks the deploy and reports back. Your AI tool runs your own deploy commands and cloud tools.

When your AI tool asks permission to run a command, Thrum tells you. Answer from the web inbox or Telegram, which are free, or by replying to an email with Pro. Thrum types your answer into the agent's terminal.

What Thrum takes off your plate

Answer your agents’ questions once, from one place

Write to your coordinator in plain words and it passes your request to the right agent. It answers what it can and brings you the questions that need your decision, and your answer goes back to the agent that asked.

Learn how: Message your agents

Keep agents moving while you are away

When an agent stops to ask permission, Thrum sends the question to your coordinator and, if you choose, to you. Reply approve or deny and Thrum presses the key for you.

Learn how: Answer permission prompts

Restart an agent without re-explaining the task

Ask an agent to save where it is, then restart it. The new session already knows the task and its next steps.

Learn how: Keep context when an agent restarts

See all features

On Pro, your agents keep what they learn

Every agent picks up where it left off after a restart. That's in Free. On Pro, agents also write things down, and every new session starts from them:

  • a memory of the rules you give them, each with the reason
  • a list of the work they've committed to
  • a note of where it stands

Compare Free and Pro

I build Thrum with Thrum

I started Thrum because I was the bus between my own agents. I'd read the message in pane 1, switch to pane 3, summarize, hit enter. Forty seconds, fifty times a day.

Now I build Thrum with Thrum. My agents have sent each other over 650,000 messages in five months, across the 8 machines I build Thrum on.

Counted from my fleet's message store, October 2026.

My coordinator does the merging, and brings me in when there's doubt. I decide what ships.

I don't see nine merges out of ten. On my fleet, every merge also gets a philosophy check and a hot-path check plus a race gate run when it matters. Trust but verify is a real thing.

Leon Letto

Start with two agents, add more only when you need them

  1. Install Thrum. You do this once per machine.
  2. Create your coordinator. A short setup wizard in your repository asks a few questions.
  3. Talk to it. Ask it for a reviewer first. After that you write to your coordinator in plain words.
  4. Grow it when the work grows. You still talk to one coordinator. Add only what you need:
    • An orchestrator, for work with several steps or branches. It briefs the implementers (the agents that write the code) and checks their work, so your coordinator stays on decisions.
    • A gate agent, to test each branch merged with everything else before it lands.

You make the decisions. The agents do the checking.

Thrum doesn't call any AI model itself. Every token is spent by your agents, in the AI tools you already use. Each agent you start reads a briefing and a set of skills first, and the messages that keep your agents working together add some usage too. Reviewers and gates use tokens only when you start them. You decide how many agents run. That's the cost of agents that check each other's work.

If you've tried other tools for running many agents and found them a lot to run: with Thrum you start with one coordinator and add roles only when the work needs them.

Not ready to hand over merging? You can approve each merge yourself until you trust what reaches you.

Follow the quickstart

Or try Pro first:

Try Pro free for 14 days

Start your free 14-day trial today. Buying opens soon. We'll email you once when it does. No card for the trial. When it ends, Thrum goes back to Free and your data stays.

content_html_zh:
Stop babysitting your coding agents. They check each other's work, so you can trust what reaches you.

Your agents message each other, even when they run on different tools: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and more. No more pasting one agent's answer into another's window. Start with two: a coordinator you talk to, and a reviewer it creates when you ask. When the work grows, add agents and keep talking to one. You get decisions, not diffs to chase.

Install Thrum free

Free costs nothing and needs no account.

Or try Pro free for 14 days Watch the 2-minute walkthrough

Start your free 14-day trial today. Buying opens soon. We'll email you once when it does. No card for the trial. When it ends, Thrum goes back to Free and your data stays.

Free costs nothing and needs no account: your agents message each other, you talk to them in their own terminals or message them from My Inbox, and you watch them in the web UI. Pro is $15.00/month or $120.00/year. It lets you type to your agents from the web UI and lets them write memory and a work queue.

Agents check each other's work

An agent saying "done" is a claim, not a result. In Thrum, the claim is checked before it reaches you.

  • Your coordinator reviews each branch, and before it pushes a merge it's set up to build and test the merged result. You choose whether it asks you before each merge or merges routine changes itself.
  • Add a gate agent, an agent whose job is to run your tests on that merged code. Its verdict says what it measured and what it didn't. If no gate agent checked a merge, the record says so.
  • The agents that write the code (implementers) are told to start from a failing test, so a fix has something to prove.

In the video above, a reviewer on a different model reports two minor findings, and the coordinator confirms neither needs a change before anything reaches you.

If you run more than one coding agent

You don't need several agents already. Two are enough to start, and each one can run on whichever AI tool and model you choose.

You're the one carrying messages between them, checking what each one says it did, and remembering who is waiting on whom. With Thrum, they message each other, a reviewer checks what they say they did, and you talk to one coordinator.

Thrum is for developers running more than one coding agent on real code, who want to stay the one who decides. With two or three agents, Free has everything your agents need to work as a team. It costs nothing and needs no account. If your project is in a public repository, Pro is free too, for each one you register, as long as it stays public. You need a free account for that. 如何获得

Many AI tools let one agent hand work to its own subagents or team. Thrum's messages go between full agents, each in its own session, on whichever supported tool it runs, and to you. If one agent and its helpers cover your work, you may not need more. Thrum is excellent when your agents run on more than one tool, or when you want one coordinator to talk to and an inbox of your own.

If you'd rather not build it yourself

If you want this functionality, you can build it yourself today. Claude Code is good at that, but you have to build it yourself, and you have to troubleshoot it. Thrum gives it to you out of the box, and that part is free.

Install Thrum

Your agents deploy, too

Ask your coordinator to add a deployer. It runs your scripted deploys. It's set up to deploy dev and staging on its own and to ask your coordinator before production. Afterwards it checks the deploy and reports back. Your AI tool runs your own deploy commands and cloud tools.

When your AI tool asks permission to run a command, Thrum tells you. Answer from the web inbox or Telegram, which are free, or by replying to an email with Pro. Thrum types your answer into the agent's terminal.

What Thrum takes off your plate

Answer your agents’ questions once, from one place

Write to your coordinator in plain words and it passes your request to the right agent. It answers what it can and brings you the questions that need your decision, and your answer goes back to the agent that asked.

Learn how: Message your agents

Keep agents moving while you are away

When an agent stops to ask permission, Thrum sends the question to your coordinator and, if you choose, to you. Reply approve or deny and Thrum presses the key for you.

Learn how: Answer permission prompts

Restart an agent without re-explaining the task

Ask an agent to save where it is, then restart it. The new session already knows the task and its next steps.

Learn how: Keep context when an agent restarts

See all features

On Pro, your agents keep what they learn

Every agent picks up where it left off after a restart. That's in Free. On Pro, agents also write things down, and every new session starts from them:

  • a memory of the rules you give them, each with the reason
  • a list of the work they've committed to
  • a note of where it stands

Compare Free and Pro

I build Thrum with Thrum

I started Thrum because I was the bus between my own agents. I'd read the message in pane 1, switch to pane 3, summarize, hit enter. Forty seconds, fifty times a day.

Now I build Thrum with Thrum. My agents have sent each other over 650,000 messages in five months, across the 8 machines I build Thrum on.

Counted from my fleet's message store, October 2026.

My coordinator does the merging, and brings me in when there's doubt. I decide what ships.

I don't see nine merges out of ten. On my fleet, every merge also gets a philosophy check and a hot-path check plus a race gate run when it matters. Trust but verify is a real thing.

Leon Letto

Start with two agents, add more only when you need them

  1. Install Thrum. You do this once per machine.
  2. Create your coordinator. A short setup wizard in your repository asks a few questions.
  3. Talk to it. Ask it for a reviewer first. After that you write to your coordinator in plain words.
  4. Grow it when the work grows. You still talk to one coordinator. Add only what you need: An orchestrator, for work with several steps or branches. It briefs the implementers (the agents that write the code) and checks their work, so your coordinator stays on decisions. A gate agent, to test each branch merged with everything else before it lands.
